title: Chiang Mai Craft Villages 2026 — Bo Sang, San Kamphaeng, Wua Lai | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: Visit Chiang Mai's craft villages: Bo Sang umbrellas, the San Kamphaeng handicraft road, and Wua Lai silversmiths around Wat Sri Suphan. With how to get there, prices, opening hours, and real half-day and full-day routes you can actually follow.
keywords: Chiang Mai craft villages, Bo Sang umbrella, San Kamphaeng, Wua Lai silver, Wat Sri Suphan, Chiang Mai handicrafts
h1:
Chiang Mai Craft Villages
Bo Sang Umbrellas, San Kamphaeng, Wua Lai Silver
intro: Chiang Mai is more than temples and cafes. Head east out of the old city for just about 10 kilometres and you reach villages where people have made things by hand for generations — saa-paper umbrellas at Bo Sang, the craftsmen's road of San Kamphaeng, and silversmiths over two hundred years old in the Wua Lai quarter right in town. This is the guide to how you get there, what to see, and how to plan a route that's worth your time.

blocks.html: Handicrafts are a root of Chiang Mai that plenty of people walk straight past without noticing. Umbrella makers, silversmiths, weavers, and wood carvers have clustered into villages here since the Lanna era. Three main spots draw most visitors: Bo Sang (saa-paper umbrellas), the San Kamphaeng road (a mix of many crafts), and the Wua Lai quarter in town (silverwork). You can do all three in a single day if you plan the route well — we'll take them one at a time.

blocks.text: Bo Sang — the saa-paper umbrella village

blocks.html: Bo Sang sits on Route 1014 in San Kamphaeng district, about 9–12 kilometres east of the old city. The whole village is known for handmade saa-paper umbrellas and fans, and the Bo Sang umbrella has become one of Chiang Mai's symbols. The place to start is the Bo Sang Umbrella Making Centre, because behind the showroom there's a workshop yard where you can watch every stage — building the bamboo frame, stretching the saa paper, right through to painting the designs by hand.

items: Opening hours — the Bo Sang Umbrella Making Centre is open daily, roughly 8:30–17:00.
Entry — walking around the village and watching the umbrella-making is free, no admission fee.
Paint-your-own workshop — painting your own umbrella runs around 1,100 THB, while painting a design on a small item such as a phone case, bag, or fan starts in the low hundreds of THB.
Time needed — an easy walk-through takes about 2–3 hours, including time to sit and watch the painters.

blocks.html: Beyond umbrellas, Bo Sang also has other crafts mixed into the shops around it — fans, silk, silverware, and carved wood. Most prices are negotiable, and buying several pieces usually brings the price down. To be honest, some shops sell stock brought in from elsewhere rather than made on site. If you want genuinely handmade pieces, pick the shops where you can see the maker at work out front.

blocks.title: The busiest time
blocks.html: Come in mid-January and you'll hit the Bo Sang Umbrella Festival — in 2026 it runs 16–18 January. The whole street is hung with hundreds of umbrellas, with a parade of women cycling and holding red umbrellas in Lanna dress, performances, and craft demonstrations from villages around San Kamphaeng. It's crowded, but the most photogenic time of the year.

blocks.text: San Kamphaeng — the road of many crafts

blocks.html: If Bo Sang is umbrellas, the San Kamphaeng road (continuing east from Bo Sang) is where nearly every craft Chiang Mai makes comes together. Each roadside workshop tends to specialise in just one thing, and you can walk in and watch the makers at work — silk weaving, teak carving, pottery, lacquerware, and silverwork. Most are free to visit, with no admission fee.

items.name: Handwoven silk & cotton
items.blurb: Weaving houses where you can watch the whole process from reeling silk to finished cloth — scarves, dress fabric, and home decor, with something for every budget.

items.name: Wood carving & lacquerware
items.blurb: Hand-carved teak and gilded lacquerware, good for larger home pieces, with shipping available at some shops.

items.name: Pottery & ceramics
items.blurb: Bowls, vases, and northern-style glazed ware, from small souvenirs to collector pieces.

blocks.title: Getting around
blocks.html: The workshops along the San Kamphaeng road are kilometres apart — too far to walk between. Rent a motorbike or hire a red songthaew to wait for you and you'll move around far more easily, and most shops have their own parking.

blocks.text: Wua Lai — the silver quarter in town

blocks.html: You don't even have to leave town for old-school crafts. The Wua Lai quarter, south of the old city, has been a silversmiths' neighbourhood for over two hundred years. Silver and lacquerware artisans migrated here from Shan State and settled the area, and silver workshops still run here into the present generation. The heart of the quarter is Wat Sri Suphan, home to the only all-silver ordination hall in Thailand, every pattern hand-embossed by the community's silversmiths.

items: Wat Sri Suphan — 100 Wua Lai Road, 50 THB to view the silver ordination hall (includes a souvenir keyring and a bottle of water).
Good to know — women may visit the temple grounds, but by tradition are not allowed inside the silver ordination hall itself.
Saturday nights — the Wua Lai walking street runs in front of the temple, the silver hall stays open until around 21:30, and there's a light-and-sound show on the hall.
What you can buy — handmade silverware, jewellery, and embossed pieces, bought directly from the makers in the lanes around the temple.

blocks.html: Come on a Saturday night and you get crafts, northern street food, and the walking-street atmosphere all in one place — but be warned, it's packed on Saturday evenings. If you'd rather look at silverwork quietly and actually chat with the makers, try a weekday afternoon instead.

blocks.text: Suggested routes — half day and full day

blocks.html: You can plan these three stops two ways. Short on time? Do a half day on just the eastern side (Bo Sang + San Kamphaeng). Have the whole day? Finish with Wua Lai in the evening.

blocks.label: Plan A
blocks.title: Half day on the eastern craft road

items.activity: Leave the old city for Bo Sang
items.note: About 25–30 min by car or motorbike, or a white songthaew from Warorot Market for around 30 THB

items.activity: Bo Sang Umbrella Making Centre — watch every stage of umbrella-making
items.note: Want to paint your own umbrella? Allow extra time and around 1,100 THB

items.activity: Move on to the San Kamphaeng road, walk through the weaving and woodwork houses
items.note: Pick 2–3 workshops to stop at — don't try to see them all

items.activity: Lunch around San Kamphaeng, then head back to town
items.note: Plenty of local spots here for khao soi and northern food

blocks.label: Plan B
blocks.title: Full day, adding Wua Lai in the evening

items.activity: Follow Plan A — Bo Sang + San Kamphaeng
items.note: Head back into town in the afternoon to rest first

items.activity: Visit Wat Sri Suphan and the silver ordination hall
items.note: 50 THB entry — the late-afternoon sun makes the silver glow

items.activity: Walk the silversmiths' lanes around Wua Lai and chat with the makers
items.note: Weekdays are quieter, so you can look at the work closely

items.activity: If it's a Saturday, carry on to the Wua Lai walking street + light show on the hall
items.note: Crowded — allow extra time to find parking

items: Prices are negotiable — most crafts in the villages can be bargained, especially if you buy several pieces.
Look for the real handmade pieces — choose shops where you can see the maker working out front, to avoid stock brought in to resell.
Bring cash — many small shops take cash only, though some accept QR payment.
Dress for the temple — for Wat Sri Suphan, dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered.

faq.q: How do you get to Chiang Mai's craft villages?
faq.a: Bo Sang and San Kamphaeng are about 9–13 kilometres east of the old city. Take a white songthaew from Warorot Market (Kad Luang) for around 30 THB, roughly half an hour, or rent a motorbike / hire a red songthaew for more flexibility. The Wua Lai quarter is in town, walkable from the old city.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee to watch the umbrella-making at Bo Sang?
faq.a: No entry fee — you can walk around the village and watch the umbrella makers at the Bo Sang Umbrella Making Centre for free. It's open daily, roughly 8:30–17:00. If you want to paint your own umbrella there's a workshop for around 1,100 THB, while painting a design on a small item starts in the low hundreds of THB.

faq.q: How much is entry to Wat Sri Suphan (the silver temple)?
faq.a: It's 50 THB to view the silver ordination hall, including a souvenir keyring and a bottle of water. Women may enter the temple grounds but by tradition cannot go inside the hall itself. On Saturday nights it stays open until around 21:30, with a light-and-sound show.

faq.q: When is the Bo Sang Umbrella Festival in 2026?
faq.a: In 2026 it runs 16–18 January at Bo Sang in San Kamphaeng district, with the street hung with hundreds of umbrellas, a parade of women cycling and holding red umbrellas in Lanna dress, and craft demonstrations from villages around San Kamphaeng.

faq.q: How many hours does it take to visit the craft villages?
faq.a: Bo Sang alone takes about 2–3 hours. Adding San Kamphaeng fills a half day, and if you want to add Wua Lai in the evening you should set aside the whole day.
